title: Distributed Systems Reliability: CAP, Consistency, Quorums and Resilience Patterns
summary: Quick revision notes on CAP and PACELC, strong vs eventual consistency, quorums, and the resilience toolkit (rate limiting, circuit breakers, retries with backoff), closing with availability nines.

chapters.title: CAP and PACELC Mental Model
points: CAP: under a network partition a system must choose Consistency (every read sees the latest write) or Availability (every non-failed node answers); partitions are unavoidable, so the real choice is CP vs AP
CP system (e.g. etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase): minority side of a partition rejects requests or errors out to stay correct
AP system (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB default, Riak): both sides keep serving and diverge, then reconcile after the partition heals
PACELC: if Partition then choose A or C; Else (normal operation) choose Latency or Consistency; it explains why even healthy systems trade speed for freshness
Mistake: 'pick 2 of 3' is wrong; CA is not a real option for a distributed system, and CAP says nothing about behavior when there is no partition

chapters.title: Strong vs Eventual Consistency
points: Strong (linearizable) consistency: after a write returns, every later read anywhere sees it; costs cross-node coordination and higher latency
Eventual consistency: replicas converge if writes stop, but reads can return stale data in the meantime
Middle models: read-your-writes, monotonic reads and causal consistency give users a sane view without full linearizability
Convergence tools: last-write-wins (clock-dependent, can lose writes), vector clocks, CRDTs, read repair and anti-entropy
Mistake: using eventual consistency for balances, inventory or uniqueness checks; use strong consistency there and eventual for feeds, likes and counters

chapters.title: Quorums: R, W and N
points: N = replica count, W = acks needed for a write, R = replicas consulted for a read
Strong read rule: R + W > N guarantees the read set overlaps the latest write set
Example N=3: W=2,R=2 is balanced and tolerates 1 failure; W=3,R=1 is fast reads but slow writes that fail if any replica is down; W=1,R=3 is fast writes
Majority quorum = floor(N/2)+1; a cluster of 2f+1 nodes survives f failures, so use odd sizes (5 nodes tolerate 2, 6 nodes still only 2)
Mistake: R+W>N alone is not linearizable with sloppy quorums, hinted handoff or clock-based last-write-wins conflict resolution

chapters.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms
points: Purpose: protect a service from overload and abuse by capping requests per client per time window; reject with HTTP 429 plus a Retry-After header
Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a capacity, each request spends one; allows bursts up to the bucket size (most common choice)
Leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate through a queue; smooths output, no bursts
Fixed window counter is simple but allows a 2x burst at window boundaries; sliding window log is exact but memory heavy; sliding window counter approximates cheaply
Mistake: keeping counters per app instance; use a shared store like Redis with atomic INCR or a Lua script, and key by user, API key or IP

chapters.title: Circuit Breakers and Retries with Backoff
points: Circuit breaker states: Closed (calls pass, failures counted) → Open (fail fast after threshold, no calls) → Half-Open (after a timeout, allow a few probes; success closes, failure reopens)
Breaker tuning: failure-rate threshold over a rolling window, open duration, probe count; fail fast with a fallback or cached response
Retry with exponential backoff: wait base * 2^attempt, capped at a max (e.g. 100ms, 200ms, 400ms ... cap 10s) with a max attempt count
Add jitter (randomize the delay, e.g. full jitter = random(0, backoff)) so clients do not retry in synchronized waves
Mistake: retrying non-idempotent calls without an idempotency key, retrying 4xx errors, or stacking retries at every layer (3 layers x 3 tries = 27 calls) which causes a retry storm

chapters.title: Availability Nines Cheat Sheet
points: 99% = 3.65 days downtime per year; 99.9% = 8.76 hours; 99.99% = 52.6 minutes; 99.999% = 5.26 minutes
Per month: 99.9% ≈ 43.8 minutes; 99.99% ≈ 4.4 minutes
Serial dependencies multiply: two 99.9% services in a chain give about 99.8%; parallel redundancy gives 1 - (1-a)^n, so two 99.9% replicas give 99.9999%
Each extra nine costs roughly 10x more effort; SLO (internal target) must be stricter than the SLA (contractual promise), and error budget = 100% minus SLO
Cheat sheet: CP = correct but may refuse, AP = always answers but may be stale; R+W>N for strong reads; token bucket for bursts; breaker Closed→Open→Half-Open; backoff = base*2^n plus jitter
